```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_dplyr <- requireNamespace("dplyr", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(skatR)
```

Skat is a three-handed trick-taking game played across the German-speaking
world. One player -- the *declarer* -- takes on the other two, having first won
an auction for the right to name the game. This vignette walks through the
package in the order the game itself unfolds: the deck, the ordering the game
type imposes on it, the deal, the play, the bidding arithmetic, and finally
simulation and exact analysis.

## The deck

Skat uses a 32-card deck: sevens through aces in four suits. The card points
(jacks 2, queens 3, kings 4, tens 10, aces 11) sum to 120, and 61 of them wins
a suit or grand game.

```{r}
sk_full_deck()
sum(sk_points(sk_full_deck()))
```

## Trick-taking order depends on the game type

This is where Skat differs most from other trick-taking games. In suit and
grand games all four jacks are trumps, ranked clubs > spades > hearts >
diamonds, and the jack of clubs is always the strongest card in the pack. In a
suit game the named suit joins them as trumps below the jacks.

```{r}
tail(sk_card_order("grand"), 4)   # the strongest four cards
sk_is_trump(c("CJ", "HJ", "HA"), game_type = "hearts")
```

Because a jack is a trump rather than a card of its printed suit, leading one
demands a trump from the other players. `sk_effective_suit()` is the function
that encodes this, using `"T"` for trump, and `sk_legal_moves()` applies it:

```{r}
sk_effective_suit(c("CJ", "HA", "D10"), game_type = "hearts")
sk_legal_moves(c("HA", "H7", "CJ", "DA"), led = "SJ", game_type = "hearts")
```

Null games are the exception: no trumps at all, and the ten drops back to its
natural place between the nine and the jack.

```{r}
head(sk_card_order("null"), 8)
sk_trick_winner(c("H10", "HJ", "H9"), game_type = "null")
```

## Dealing and playing a game

`sk_deal()` deals ten cards to each seat plus a two-card skat. `sk_play_game()`
plays all ten tricks and scores the result.

```{r}
deal <- sk_deal(seed = 42)
deal

game <- sk_play_game(deal$hands, deal$skat, declarer = 1, game_type = "grand")
game$result
```

The game object keeps the tricks, so the play can be inspected afterwards:

```{r}
game$tricks[[1]]
game$declarer_points
```

## Bidding values

The game value combines a base value (diamonds 9 up to grand 24) with a matador
("Spitzen") multiplier: the unbroken run of top trumps the declarer holds, or
lacks, counting down from the jack of clubs.

```{r}
sk_matadors(c("CJ", "SJ", "HA", "HK", "H10"), game_type = "hearts")
sk_game_value(c("CJ", "SJ", "HA", "HK", "H10"), game_type = "hearts")
```

Null games ignore all of that and use four fixed values instead.

```{r}
sk_game_value(character(0), game_type = "null")
sk_game_value(character(0), game_type = "null", ouvert = TRUE)
```

## Simulation

`sk_simulate()` deals and plays many games, returning one tidy row per game.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
sim <- sk_simulate(n = 200, game_type = "grand", seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
mean(sim$won)
sk_plot_points(sim)
```

Because the result is a plain tibble, summarising it needs nothing special:

```{r, eval = has_dplyr}
library(dplyr)

sim |>
  group_by(won) |>
  summarise(games = n(), mean_points = mean(declarer_points))
```

Comparing game types is a matter of binding a few runs together:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
runs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  c("grand", "clubs", "hearts"),
  function(gt) sk_simulate(n = 100, game_type = gt, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
))
sk_plot_winrate(runs)
```

## Exact endgame analysis

`sk_solve_dd()` computes, by exhaustive alpha-beta search in C++, the maximum
card points the declarer can guarantee against perfect defence, given that
every hand is known. The total includes the points on the declarer's own cards.

```{r}
hands <- list(c("CJ", "SA"), c("HA", "H9"), c("DA", "D9"))
sk_solve_dd(hands, game_type = "grand", declarer = 1)
```

The search is exponential in the number of cards left, so it is above all a
tool for endgames. A two-trick hearts position, worked by hand below, is
instant:

```{r}
# Declarer leads HJ (a trump); seat 2 must follow with H7 and seat 3, holding
# no trump, throws its cheaper diamond. The declarer then leads C7 into seat
# 2's ace and loses the second trick. Total: 2 + 0 + 10.
sk_solve_dd(
  list(c("HJ", "C7"), c("H7", "CA"), c("DA", "D10")),
  game_type = "hearts", declarer = 1, leader = 1
)
```

Alpha-beta pruning, move ordering and a transposition table keep the cost down,
but only so far, so `sk_solve_dd()` refuses positions deeper than `max_tricks`
(eight cards per hand by default) rather than disappearing into a search you did
not intend to start. Whole ten-trick deals are within reach if you raise the
guard and are willing to wait: most solve in well under a second, awkward ones
in tens of seconds.

```{r}
deal <- sk_deal(seed = 1)
sk_solve_dd(deal$hands, game_type = "grand", declarer = 1, max_tricks = 10)
```

## Rule variants

`sk_ruleset()` collects the options that separate tournament play from a casual
round.

```{r}
sk_ruleset("tournament")
sk_ruleset("casual", bock = TRUE)
```

## An interactive demo

`sk_run_app()` launches a small Shiny application that runs simulations and
plots the results; it needs the suggested **shiny** package.
